A.assessment: Section A has strong coverage of core financial reporting topics with a reasonable 48/47 Apply/Understand split. Lease accounting (ASC 842), income taxes (ASC 740), and business combinations each have at least one full 5-item rotation group — better than initially assumed. However, derivatives/hedging and software costs are completely absent. The 0% Analyze/Evaluate rate across all 370 items means no items require data interpretation or professional judgment — candidates drill procedure execution but never face the 'what does this ratio mean' or 'which accounting treatment is most appropriate' questions that appear on the actual CMA exam.

E.assessment: Section E has the broadest range of topics at 206 unique topic roots (boosted by 40 R-series items in Pack E). However, the cognitive distribution is alarmingly skewed: 68.7% Understand vs. only 26.3% Apply. This means nearly 7 in 10 items test recall/recognition of definitions rather than application of control frameworks to scenarios. For a section where the CMA exam heavily tests scenario-based control assessment and risk evaluation, this is a serious depth gap. COSO ERM coverage at 21 items is a positive finding. Fraud prevention is covered but fraud detection is absent. The 415-item total (vs 370-375 in other sections) partially offsets the shallow cognitive profile.

F.assessment: Section F has the widest topic scope (200 unique topic roots) but the shallowest cognitive profile of any section: 84.5% Understand, 14.7% Apply. Only 1 item in the entire section is labeled 'Analyze'. The template-based authoring produces 'Company X is evaluating Y in a finance transformation project. Which response is most appropriate?' stems that test recognition, not application. Every emerging technology (blockchain, AI, RPA, cloud, IoT) has a presence — but at the definitional level only. The 374 items provide token coverage of modern topics without the simulation-level practice (scenario-based data governance decisions, analytics method selection, security control design) that the CMA exam increasingly demands.

topic_density_concerns.concern: Highest-density single topic in the entire question bank. 16 items on one budget schedule is excessive — candidates get 16x more practice on DM purchasing than on Monte Carlo simulation (1 item).

COSO Principle labels at 16 items likely represent two rotation groups of the same template pattern. While core to the CMA exam, this density at the Understand level crowds out control scenario application.

21 items on service dept allocation (direct/step/reciprocal) is the highest density in Section D. While a tested topic, this may be disproportionate for a 15% section — candidates spend disproportionate practice time on allocation mechanics vs. modern cost management.

15 items labeled simply 'variance analysis' with no topic specialization. The rotation-group template produces mechanically-varied items without specific variance-type focus, diluting educational value compared to labeled material/labor/OH variance items.

91 keyword hits for AI/ML — but nearly all follow the 'Company X is evaluating Y in a finance transformation project' template at Understand level. High token count masks low cognitive depth. Candidates may memorize AI definitions across 91 items without ever applying which analytics method fits a given business problem.

Section F is 84.5% Understand level — nearly a pure definition-matching section. 14.7% Apply and 0.3% Analyze is catastrophically low for a section that the CMA exam increasingly tests at the application and analysis level.

Section E is 68.7% Understand — nearly 7 in 10 items test recall rather than application. The CMA exam heavily tests internal control scenario assessment, which requires Apply/Analyze items. The current pool is definition-heavy.

cognitive_level_crisis.summary: Across all 2,534 items in the question bank, Analyze coverage is effectively zero (0.0% to 0.8% per section). Evaluate coverage is 0.0% across all sections. The CAQS v1.0 target distribution is 40% Apply, 25% Analyze, 15% Evaluate. The current distribution is fundamentally incompatible with this target.

by_section.A: 48% Apply, 47% Understand — closest to healthy balance but missing Analyze entirely
by_section.B: 66% Apply, 29% Understand — best Apply ratio, but 0.2% Analyze is functionally zero

cognitive_level_crisis.root_cause: The 5-item rotation-group template engine assigns cognitive level by position in the rotation group (pos 1=Remember, pos 2-3=Understand, pos 4-5=Apply) without assessing the actual cognitive demand of the item. This produces mechanically-labeled items that are often at the wrong cognitive level. Additionally, the template format ('Company X is evaluating Y. Which response is most appropriate?') intrinsically favors recognition over application.

structural_observations.finding: 5-item rotation group template produces broad but shallow coverage
structural_observations.detail: Every topic area gets exactly one 5-item rotation group (or occasionally two). This ensures baseline exposure to every topic but prevents depth. Advanced topics (derivatives, prescriptive analytics, fraud detection) that didn't make it into the rotation template get 0 items.
structural_observations.impact: Topic coverage is broad at the topic-root level (180-285 unique topics per section) but thin at the per-topic level (most topics have exactly 5 items — one rotation group)

structural_observations.finding: Topic labeling is rotation-group variant, not cognitive scaffold
structural_observations.detail: Section C: 'variance analysis' repeated 15 times with no sub-topic distinction. Section A: 'accounting equation equity calculation 1' through 'accounting equation equity calculation 20' — the numeric suffix indicates rotation position, not pedagogical sequencing.
structural_observations.impact: Makes blueprint coverage audit difficult — labels don't distinguish between items that test different aspects of the same topic

structural_observations.finding: Section E has 415 items (40 extra via Pack E R-series)
structural_observations.detail: Pack E Section E contains 115 items vs. standard 75 — includes P1-E-R01 through P1-E-R40 supplemented items. These boost total Section E to 415 vs. 370-375 in other sections.
structural_observations.impact: R-series items partially offset Section E's shallow cognitive profile but their quality and consistency with main-section items needs verification

structural_observations.finding: Pack D Section F has 74 items (vs. 75 in other sections)
structural_observations.detail: Confirmed 1 item missing in Pack D Section F relative to the standard 75-item section template.
structural_observations.impact: Minor — 1 item does not materially affect Section F coverage. Likely a template-rotation omission.

structural_observations.finding: Zero Evaluate-level items across all 2,534 items
structural_observations.detail: Not a single item in any section is labeled 'Evaluate' — the highest Bloom's level that requires professional judgment, recommendation formulation, and decision-making under uncertainty.
structural_observations.impact: The question bank cannot prepare candidates for the CMA exam's most challenging items. Evaluate items are typically the differentiators between passing and failing candidates.
